title: Computing Products Without Self Inclusion

phrases.explanation: A constraint meaning you cannot use the divide operator to solve the problem
Prefix means elements before a position, suffix means elements after a position

concept: Given an integer array nums, return an array result where result[i] is the product of all elements in nums except nums[i]. You must solve it without using the division operator.

solutions.label: Brute Force with Nested Loops
solutions.summary: For each index, loop through all other indices and multiply their values together.

solutions.label: Prefix and Suffix Arrays
solutions.summary: Build a prefix product array and a suffix product array, then multiply them element by element.

solutions.label: Optimized Single Output Array
solutions.summary: Use the output array to store prefix products, then sweep backward with a running suffix variable.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Clarification
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Input: nums = [1,2,3,4]"] --> B["For index 0: 2×3×4 = 24"]
    A --> C["For index 1: 1×3×4 = 12"]
    A --> D["For index 2: 1×2×4 = 8"]
    A --> E["For index 3: 1×2×3 = 6"]
    B --> F["Output: [24,12,8,6]"]
    C --> F
    D --> F
    E --> F
    style A fill:#f87171,color:#000
    style F fill:#f87171,color:#000

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here is today's problem. You are given an integer array. Return a new array where each element equals the product of every other element in the original array, except the one at that same index. Oh, and one important constraint: you cannot use division.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let me confirm. For the array one, two, three, four, the result at index zero would be two times three times four, which is twenty-four. Is that correct?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. And the full output would be twenty-four, twelve, eight, six. The array will have at least two elements and can be up to one hundred thousand elements long. Values can be negative or zero.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. Can there be zeros in the array? That would normally make division tricky, which I guess is why division is banned.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, zeros are possible. The no-division rule is a firm constraint, not just a hint. The answer is guaranteed to fit in a thirty-two-bit integer.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So I need to compute, for each index, the product of all elements except itself, without division, handling zeros and negatives. Let me think about approaches.

sections.title: Brute Force with Nested Loops
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Pick index i"] --> B["Loop j from 0 to n-1"]
    B --> C{"Is j equal to i?"}
    C -->|Yes| D["Skip this element"]
    C -->|No| E["Multiply into product"]
    D --> B
    E --> B
    B --> F["Store product at result i"]
    F --> G["Repeat for all i"]
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#000
    style F fill:#60a5fa,color:#000
    style G fill:#60a5fa,color:#000

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest approach is brute force. For each index i, I loop through every other index j, skipping when j equals i, and multiply all those values together. This gives the correct product for each position.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What is the time complexity of that approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: It is O of n-squared because for each of the n elements, I iterate through n minus one others. Space is O of n for the output array only.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That works but is too slow for large inputs. Can you do better than n-squared?

sections.title: Prefix and Suffix Product Arrays
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Input
    N["nums: [1, 2, 3, 4]"]
    end
    subgraph Prefix
    P["prefix: [1, 1, 2, 6]"]
    end
    subgraph Suffix
    S["suffix: [24, 12, 4, 1]"]
    end
    subgraph Result
    R["result: [24, 12, 8, 6]"]
    end
    N --> P
    N --> S

    style P fill:#a78bfa,color:#000
    style S fill:#a78bfa,color:#000
    style R fill:#a78bfa,color:#000

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I can observe that the product at index i equals the product of everything to its left times the product of everything to its right. So I will build two arrays: a prefix array and a suffix array.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The prefix array stores cumulative products from left to right. Prefix of zero is one. Prefix of one is nums zero. Prefix of two is nums zero times nums one, and so on.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The suffix array stores cumulative products from right to left. Then result at i equals prefix of i multiplied by suffix of i. Each pass is O of n, so total time is O of n.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good improvement. The time is now O of n, but you are using two extra arrays. Can you reduce the extra space?

sections.title: Optimized Single Output Array
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Pass 1: Left to Right"] --> B["Store prefix products in result array"]
    B --> C["result = [1, 1, 2, 6]"]
    C --> D["Pass 2: Right to Left"]
    D --> E["Multiply each result element by running suffix"]
    E --> F["result = [24, 12, 8, 6]"]
    style A fill:#fb923c,color:#000
    style D fill:#fb923c,color:#000
    style F fill:#fb923c,color:#000

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I can eliminate the extra arrays entirely. First, I fill the result array with prefix products using a left-to-right pass. Result at zero starts as one, and each next position stores the running product of all elements before it.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Then I sweep from right to left, keeping a single variable called suffix that tracks the running product from the right. At each index, I multiply result of i by suffix, then update suffix by multiplying in nums of i.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: This gives O of n time with O of one extra space, since the output array does not count as extra space. We only use one integer variable for the suffix running product.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Excellent. Walk me through the example one, two, three, four.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: After the left pass, result is one, one, two, six. Then the right pass: suffix starts at one. Index three: result stays six, suffix becomes four. Index two: two times four is eight, suffix becomes twelve. Index one: one times twelve is twelve, suffix becomes twenty-four. Index zero: one times twenty-four is twenty-four. Final result: twenty-four, twelve, eight, six.

sections.title: Summary and Comparison
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Comparison
    A["Brute Force\nO of n-squared time\nO of n space"] --> B["Prefix-Suffix Arrays\nO of n time\nO of n space"]
    B --> C["Optimized\nO of n time\nO of one space"]
    end
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#000
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#000
    style C fill:#fb923c,color:#000

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great work. Let us recap. We went from O of n-squared brute force, to O of n with two extra arrays, and finally to O of n time with O of one extra space using a single output array with a running suffix variable.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key insight is that each element's answer is the product of its prefix and suffix. By computing these in two passes over the result array, we avoid both division and extra space.
